source_text: Incipiamus igitur probare nativitatem Christi a prophetis esse nuntiatam. Sic Esaias dicit: Audite, domus David, non pusillum vobis certamen cum hominibus, quoniam Deus praestat certamen: propter hoc ipse Deus dabit vobis signum: Ecce virgo concipiet in utero et pariet filium, et vocabitis nomen ejus Emmanuel, quod interpretatur: Nobiscum Deus. Butyrum et mel manducabit. Quoniam, priusquam cognoscat infans vocare patrem aut matrem, accipiet virtutem Damasci, et spolia Samariae adversus regem Assyriorum.. Itaque dicunt Judaei: Provocemus istam praedicationem Esaiae, et faciamus comparationem, an Christo qui jam venit, competat illi primo nomen quod Esaias praedicavit, et insignia ejus quae de eo nuntiavit. Equidem Esaias praedicat eum Emmanuelem vocari oportere, dehinc virtutem sumpturum Damasci et spolia Samariae adversus regem Assyriorum. Porro, inquiunt, iste qui venit, neque sub ejusmodi nomine est editus, neque re bellica functus. At nos e contrario admonendos eos existimavimus, uti cohaerentia quoque hujus capituli recognoscant: subjuncta est enim et interpretatio Emmanuel, Nobiscum Deus, uti non solum sonum nominis spectes, sed et sensum. Sonus enim hebraicus, quod est Emmanuel, suae gentis est; sensus autem ejus, quod est Deus nobiscum, ex interpretatione communis est. Quaero ergo an ista vox, Nobiscum Deus, quod est Emmanuel, exinde quo Christus inluxit, agitetur in Christo? Et puto, ex toto non negabis. Nam qui ex Judaismo credunt Christo, ex quo in eum credunt, Emmanuel cum volent dicere, nobiscum Deum esse significant. Atque ita constat jam venisse illum qui praedicabatur Emmanuel, quia quod significat Emmanuel, venit, id est Nobiscum Deus. Aeque et sono nominis inducuntur, cum virtutem Damasci, et spolia Samariae adversus regem Assyriorum, sic accipiunt, quasi bellatorem portendant Christum, non animadvertentes quid Scriptura praemittat: Quoniam priusquam cognoscat puer vocare patrem aut matrem, accipiet virtutem Damasci et spolia Samariae adversus regem Assyriorum. Ante est enim inspicias aetatis demonstrationem, an virum jam Christum exhibere ista aetas possit, nedum imperatorem; scilicet vagitu ad arma esset convocaturus infans; et signum belli, non tuba, sed crepitacillo daturus; nec ex equo vel de muro, sed de nutricis et gerulae suae dorso sive collo hostem destinaturus; atque ita Damascum et Samariam pro mammis subacturus.
pass_a_gloss: Let us begin therefore to prove that the birth of Christ was announced by the prophets. Thus Isaiah says: Hear, house of David, you have no small contest with men, since God provides the contest: for this reason God himself will give you a sign: Behold, a virgin will conceive in the womb and will bear a son, and you will call his name Emmanuel, which is interpreted: God with us. He will eat butter and honey. For, before the infant knows how to call father or mother, he will receive the power of Damascus, and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. And so the Jews say: Let us challenge this prophecy of Isaiah, and let us make a comparison, whether the first name that Isaiah prophesied fits Christ who has already come, and the signs that he announced about him. Indeed, Isaiah prophesies that he ought to be called Emmanuel, and then he will take the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. Furthermore, they say, this one who has come, neither was he brought forth under such a name, nor did he perform deeds of war. But we, on the contrary, think that they should be warned, so that they may also recognize the coherence of this chapter: for the interpretation of Emmanuel, God with us, is also added, so that you may not only consider the sound of the name, but also its meaning. For the sound of the Hebrew name, which is Emmanuel, is of his own people; but its meaning, which is God with us, is common from the interpretation. I ask, therefore, whether this phrase, God with us, which is Emmanuel, is at work in Christ from the time he shone forth? And I think you will not deny it entirely. For those who believe in Christ from Judaism, from the time they believe in him, when they want to say Emmanuel, they signify that God is with us. And so it is established that he who was prophesied as Emmanuel has already come, because what Emmanuel signifies has come, that is, God with us. Similarly, they are also led by the sound of the name, when they take the power of Damascus, and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians, as if they were portraying Christ as a warrior, not noticing what Scripture premises: For before the boy knows how to call father or mother, he will receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. For first, one must consider the demonstration of age, whether this age can already show Christ as a man, let alone an emperor; certainly, the infant would be summoned to arms with crying, and the sign of war would be given not with a trumpet, but with a rattle; and the enemy would be destined not from a horse or a wall, but from the back or neck of his nurse or carrier; and thus Damascus and Samaria would be subjugated like breasts.

pass_b_english: Let us start, then, by proving the prophets announced Christ's birth. Isaiah says: "Listen, house of David; this is no trivial dispute with mere mortals, because God himself guarantees the outcome. Therefore the Lord will give you a sign himself: Look — a virgin will conceive and bear a son, and you will name him Emmanuel, which means 'God with us'" (Isaiah 7:14). "He will eat butter and honey. For before the child knows enough to call for father or mother, he will receive the wealth of Damascus and the plunder of Samaria from the king of Assyria" (Isaiah 7:15).

The Jewish objection runs like this: Let us test Isaiah's prophecy; let us compare whether the very first name Isaiah foretold fits the Christ who has already come, along with the identifying marks attached to him. Isaiah declares he must be called Emmanuel, and afterward he will take Damascus's power and Samaria's spoils from the Assyrian king. But the one who came, they insist, was neither born under that name nor did any warrior deeds.

We, on the contrary, think they need warning so they will also grasp this chapter's coherence. The interpretation "God with us" is appended to Emmanuel precisely so you weigh not just the sound of the name but its sense. The Hebrew sound "Emmanuel" belongs to his own people; the sense "God with us," however, becomes common property through translation. So I ask: has the phrase "God with us" — which is what Emmanuel means — been operative in Christ from the moment he appeared? I think you will not deny it entirely. Jews who believe in Christ, from the moment they believe, whenever they utter "Emmanuel" signify that God is with us. Thus it stands proved that the one prophesied as Emmanuel has already come, because what Emmanuel signifies has come — namely, God with us.

They are likewise misled by the bare sound of the name when they treat the taking of Damascus's power and Samaria's spoils from the Assyrian king as a portrait of Christ the warrior, overlooking Scripture's premise: "Before the boy knows how to call father or mother, he will receive the power of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria from the king of Assyria" (Isaiah 7:15). One must first examine the age indicator: can this age even present Christ as a man, let alone an emperor? The infant would be summoned to arms by crying; the battle signal would be not a trumpet but a rattle; he would engage the enemy not from horseback or a wall but from the back or neck of his nurse or carrier; and thus Damascus and Samaria would be subdued like breasts.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a polished version that correctly incorporates the required inline scripture citations (Isaiah 7:14 and Isaiah 7:15) which were present in the source text's allusions. All nuances regarding the 'sound' vs 'sense' of the name and the 'age demonstration' are preserved.
